column2: Act Three
The Dictator
The metal doors opened and closed. The man was truly gone. In the unreal beam of light, the girl began to cry without a sound.

The little rods and spheres rolled together. Adams took shape again, chattering “Hee-ha, hee-ha, hee-ha!” It rolled over to EVA on several metal balls, waited a moment, then suddenly waved both hands above its head and shook its body in an ungainly dance. “EVA, be happy! EVA, be happy! EVA, be happy!”
Coins clattered from its hands across the floor. The girl’s tears fell onto the metal as well, splashing into faint, illusory glimmers of blue.
Late at night. Norton Hall. The conference room.

Every member of the Student Council’s executive committee was present. Caesar, the current president, sat on the sofa before the fireplace, chin propped on both hands, staring ahead. Above him hung the Gattuso family’s phoenix crest. The silence had lasted a long time. Almost everyone had their head bowed.
“For the first time in three years, we’re losing the use of Norton Hall. This will be our last meeting here,” Caesar said quietly. “For me, this is unprecedented. A crushing defeat.”

Dejection weighed on them like a mountain. Since Caesar took charge, the Student Council had always won Freedom Day. Under him, it had finally become a match for Cassell’s most traditional fraternity, the Lionheart Society. Even the appearance of Chu Zihang, the so-called super-A-rank, hadn’t cost them Norton Hall. Now, inconceivably, a freshman had beaten them.
“We didn’t lose. This was a disgraceful war of sneak attacks!” a senior committee member protested. “We shouldn’t give up Norton Hall!”
Indignation spread. The members whispered among themselves. The defeat was simply too unfair.
“Stop!” Caesar raised a hand. The authority in his voice silenced the room.

“I refuse to speak with cowards. Only cowards refuse to acknowledge defeat.” His ice-blue eyes showed no emotion. “I don’t intend to discuss why we lost. Lu Mingfei, an S-rank freshman from China, shot Chu Zihang and me and won this year’s Freedom Day as a third participant. Respect the rules. Under the rules, we lost. Lionheart has remained silent, which means Chu accepts the result. Are you inferior to Chu Zihang?”

“I’ve rented Amber Hall next door for next year’s Student Council activities. Move our belongings out. From midnight, this place belongs to Lu Mingfei.” Caesar rose and poured himself a cognac. “He should be preparing for tomorrow’s 3E exam. Do you think he’ll pass?”
“Caesar, you mean…?”
“A story just broke on the campus news site. Our S-rank freshman has no resonance with Yanling: Emperor,” Caesar said softly.
After a moment of silence, delighted surprise flashed in every member’s eyes.

“The exam results will show his potential. If he fails, he’ll be demoted. With no Yanling resonance, how can he pass?” Caesar looked around the room. “I’m looking forward to it. I imagine Chu is, too. Nono, what do you think of him?”
“That loser? Probably straight down to Z, if there is a Z-rank.” Leaning against the wall, Nono sounded unconcerned.

The committee members exchanged smiles. The 3E exam was the first hurdle, one that unsettled every freshman. Lu Mingfei wouldn’t find it so easy to keep smiling. If he failed, he would plummet through the ranks—B, C, D, E, F—and become the college’s laughingstock. A sheep slipping into a pride of lions in a lion’s skin, then being exposed: its fate scarcely bore imagining.
Caesar didn’t smile. He lowered his head and touched his chest where Lu Mingfei’s bullet had struck.

“The initials are EEE: Extraction Evaluation Exam. It means a bloodline assessment. Its main purpose is to identify students’ dragon blood. Those with dragon ancestry resonate with Draconic, producing spirit vision—Draconic characters naturally appear in their minds,” Fingel explained. “That ability is crucial. Dragon descendants possess a supernatural power called Yanling. Within their domain, words spoken in Draconic become a rule. Language is the tool dragons use to exercise their powers. Students insensitive to Draconic usually lack ability. After 3E, they’re demoted. The worst are ordered to withdraw.”
“I was practically kidnapped and sold here! Now they’ll order me to leave?” Lu Mingfei said.
“They’ll wipe your memory and throw you out. You signed the confidentiality agreement. And if you go home now, you’ll probably have to repeat your exam year, right?”
“That’s an unfair contract! He wrote it in Latin. Who the hell could read it?”

Professor Guderian wasn’t there to hear the complaint. Stumped by Lu Mingfei’s inability to resonate with Draconic, the old man had declared it an academic problem and gone to the library to research it.

The room fell quiet. The window stood open. Sitting on his bunk, Lu Mingfei watched a beautiful full moon. Its light shone on the church spire’s red tiles, and a pleasant night breeze brushed over him. What a lovely place. Tomorrow, he would be thrown out.
“Memory wipes are actually fun.” Fingel’s head dangled from the upper bunk like a hanged ghost’s.
“Never had one. Soon I’ll get to try. So happy.” Lu Mingfei was magnificently calm.

He guessed Fingel was trying to frighten him. The best counterattack was a poker face. Just as when Lu Mingze would gleefully announce over dinner, I saw Chen Wenwen browsing a bookstore with a handsome guy from Class Two. She looked so happy! Lu Mingfei would put on a blank expression and say, What? Were you talking to me, my good man? Unable to breach his thick skin, Lu Mingze could only gather the dishes and retreat in defeat.
“Didn’t some Chinese philosopher say people suffer because their memories are too good?”

“No philosopher. Ouyang Feng said it in Ashes of Time… Wipe away, wipe away. I’m definitely failing tomorrow. Wipe me clean and send me home to repeat the year. If I can’t get into college, I’ll be unemployed…” For no clear reason, he sighed.
“You just sighed,” Fingel said.
“I yawned.”
“You don’t want to go back to China,” Fingel said suddenly.
Lu Mingfei paused, not understanding.
“Nothing wrong with going back. I don’t care. Caring wouldn’t help anyway.” Hands behind his head, he leaned back and stretched.

Gripping the upper mattress, Fingel performed an extremely difficult pike maneuver and slowly lowered himself onto Lu Mingfei’s bunk. “Good to keep things in perspective. Cassell isn’t so wonderful. They call it college, but you spend your days with reptiles, then graduate and travel the world killing dragons, risking a roasting in dragonfire. You don’t look like the hot-blooded type who shouts, ‘My destiny is to roam the earth slaying mighty dragons!’ Right?”
“That’s exactly what I’m saying. I see nothing wrong with failing and going back.” Lu Mingfei looked into Fingel’s silver-gray, Aryan eyes and shrugged. “I don’t care.”
“But you just sighed,” Fingel repeated.
A scorching rush surged from Lu Mingfei’s chest, like the urge to vomit after eating something too hot. It burned and hurt, making him forget pride and pretense. He just wanted to open his mouth.

“What’s with the nagging? What do you want? What the hell do you care if I go back? You’re a loser yourself. All these years and you haven’t graduated! Think you’re impressive? You still owe me money. How many Cokes have you drunk? Pay me back or shut up!” He didn’t know why he had suddenly exploded.
He regretted it as soon as the words escaped. Fingel might be his only friend here. As for Nono, he had shot her boyfriend. She was probably with that handsome blond now.
“Brother, you’re losing your cool.” Fingel patted his shoulder.
Lu Mingfei looked at him, then lowered his head.
“You keep saying, ‘I want to withdraw, I want to withdraw,’” Fingel said. “I only wanted to understand your state of mind.”
Lu Mingfei sighed. “Sometimes I really do. But where would I go? And why haven’t you thought about quitting? What’s so great here? Eight years and no degree.”
“Would it kill you not to poke a sore spot?”
“Fine, no poking. Just talk me through your inner journey.”
“Because… I’m lonely.” Fingel shrugged.
“Lonely? You? Come on! With all your wisecracks, you’re one step from hosting a talk show.” Lu Mingfei rolled his eyes.

“I’m serious. People with dragon blood aren’t entirely human. It gives you Yanling, but also alienates you from humanity. Once you gain that power, you’re always reminded you aren’t ordinary. Only among your own kind does the loneliness disappear, so dragon descendants naturally gather together. It’s genetic. We call that loneliness blood sorrow.” Fingel paused. “Wait. You’re S-rank. Have you never felt especially… lonely?”
“Lonely?” Lu Mingfei considered his eighteen years and shook his head. “No.”

Fingel scratched his head. “At Chicago station, you were always staring into space. What were you thinking about? Your parents aren’t around, you have no strengths, no luck with girls, bad grades, not even a real buddy. It would be a cosmic injustice if you weren’t lonely,” he said. “Even I was. As a kid, I mean.”

“But what does feeling lonely do? Is loneliness some great achievement? Dwelling on it only makes you feel worse.” Lu Mingfei looked at the ceiling. “Nobody talks to you, so you’re lonely. But being lonely still won’t make anybody talk to you.”
Fingel nodded with great seriousness. “Being lonely… still won’t make anybody talk to you… That actually makes sense… Brother, you’re a philosopher.”

“You’re the philosopher. A stinging jellyfish, more like,” Lu Mingfei said. “Just find ways to kill time, and you won’t feel lonely. Spacing out alone is interesting enough. I’d sit on our roof thinking about this and that, and whoosh, the whole evening was gone.”
“Sounds like you were happy enough in China. Why not go back? Even blood sorrow doesn’t affect you.”
Lu Mingfei thought, sighed, rested his elbows on his knees, lowered his head, and clutched his hair.
“But at home,” he whispered, “I have nothing. If there were nothing at home, would you go back?” He looked at Fingel.
Fingel looked back. Something flickered in his silver-gray eyes: the sympathy of one vulnerable creature for another, or some secretion of loneliness? Lu Mingfei couldn’t tell.

“Even wild lilies get a spring. Even a little bastard wants to sprout.” He shrugged. “I may be useless, but I want people to notice me. I want girls to like me. I want something to brag about… I don’t want to spend my whole life as an extra.” His stomach growled twice.
Fingel blinked. “Hungry? Let’s order a late supper. Lend me your student ID.”
“They do late-night food?” Lu Mingfei brightened a little and handed over the card. “You don’t mean takeout tea eggs?”

“Tea eggs? It’s our first night as roommates. We need a feast!” Fingel read out the ID number. “Room 303, Area One. Two orders of truffle bread, two pan-seared foie gras with lemon juice, a bottle of champagne… Yes, an ice bucket and lemon peel. A roast goose, too. We’re a little hungry. Two herring rolls with cheese.”
Lu Mingfei wiped the corner of his mouth. His stomach celebrated with a chorus of rumbles.

Twenty minutes later, white-clad waiters wheeled in a trolley and lifted solid-silver covers, revealing Fingel’s feast on silver platters. They assembled a table in the dorm, spread a snowy cloth, laid silver knives and forks, and set the champagne bucket in the center. Two chilled glasses beaded with condensation went before the boys. Finally, they lit a candle and withdrew. Throughout, they only smiled, never making a sound.

“Wow! It really is a school for aristocrats! I was ready to quit tomorrow, but this meal’s making me reconsider.” Lu Mingfei drove his fork into the goose’s breast and happily watched the fat well out.

“Eat! A man’s iron, but food’s steel. Miss one meal and hunger’s real! Think about 3E on a full stomach. There’s always a road around the mountain. Away from home, you rely on brothers. You’ve got me!” Fingel seized the truffle bread and chewed. “Dig in!”
“You’re really fluent in those stock phrases!” Feeling better, Lu Mingfei tore off a goose leg and began chewing, grandly offering Fingel the other.
“Reading and replying on forums is the best Chinese practice!” Fingel accepted it. Across the candlelight, both grinned brilliantly.

Meanwhile, their teacher, Professor Guderian, was examining documents in the library. In the rare-books section, Burmese-hardwood shelves rose to the ceiling, their color and sheen metallic under the lights. Endless rows of huge bound volumes held transparent vacuum-sealed sleeves preserving ancient copper scrolls, collectively called the Ice Sea Fragments. Buried beneath icy seas for thousands of years, they still hadn’t been fully deciphered.
Atop a ladder, Guderian stretched his arm toward a volume.
“Researching in the middle of the night?” someone asked below.
He looked down at a round object as shiny as the overhead lights.
“Manstein? What brings you here so late?” He was surprised.
The Disciplinary Committee chairman rubbed his gleaming head. “Research, too. On your new student, Lu Mingfei.”
“Oh? Really? He’s certainly worth studying.” Guderian paused, answering vaguely.

“A freshman facing Chu Zihang’s golden dragon eyes, firing without a trace of fear. Chu has the purest dragon blood we’ve found and already exhibits a dragon’s physiological trait: dragon eyes. Most people feel awe beneath his direct gaze. Your student felt nothing. Interesting.” Manstein’s voice was cold.
“He’s S-rank. Anything can happen with an S-rank,” Guderian said hastily.
“You’re pleased with your new student. Intend to make him Cassell’s finest young man?” Manstein asked.
“Yes, yes.” Guderian smiled and scratched his head. “Then I’ll get tenure, too.”
“From our days sharing a room at Harvard until now, you’ve always scratched your head when you lie. Can’t you control it a little?” Manstein sighed.
Guderian’s expression changed. After a silence, he dutifully climbed down. “What do you know?”
“He doesn’t resonate with Yanling: Emperor. Correct?” Manstein looked directly into his eyes, his blue-gray Aryan gaze cold as metal.
“How did you know?” Guderian whispered.

“It’s tonight’s headline on the campus site. Posted by your student Fingel. ‘Breaking: S-Rank Lu Mingfei Has No Resonance with the Dragon Emperor’s Secret Incantation. College Investigates!’ Everyone knows now.”
“Fingel?” Guderian stared.

“Your specialty is dragon genealogy. Scatterbrained though you are, you’ve always been better than me at your subject. You wouldn’t jump to a conclusion like bloodline mutation. You know dragon blood is immensely powerful. Dozens of generations of interbreeding won’t erase it completely, and there hasn’t been a single mutation. Yet you told your students Lu Mingfei had mutated. From that moment, you were trying to cover it up. Correct?”

Guderian nodded. “I recited Yanling: Emperor: ‘Praise our king’s awakening. Destruction is rebirth.’ No resonance whatsoever. The only known dragon descendant unresponsive to Emperor. But he does have dragon blood. Otherwise, he could scarcely have resisted Chu’s golden eyes. That judgment isn’t based solely on the principal’s S rating.”

“Nidhogg is the sole ancestor of the dragons. Emperor is the supreme Yanling by which he rules his descendants. Any of his blood, on hearing it, feels his summons. Yet Lu Mingfei said you were singing. This is no small matter.”
Guderian was silent.
“Ice Sea Fragment AD0099. I’ve found what you need.” Manstein handed him a copper scroll sealed in a cylindrical glass vessel.
“An AD fragment?” Guderian was startled. “Top secret!”
“Only the oldest documents conceal the highest secrets,” Manstein said. “Emperor works on every bloodline that submits to the Dragon Emperor. But one bloodline does not submit.”
“The White King, mentioned in the secret chapter of the Dragon Chronicles,” Guderian whispered. “Our old joint research subject.”

“Yes. We happen to be the two people here who know its history best. The White King’s Yanling: Oracle is the only known Yanling that counters Emperor. After betraying the Black King, it used Oracle on all its own descendants.”
“You mean Lu Mingfei is… descended from the White King?”
Manstein nodded slightly. “I can think of no other explanation.”

After a long silence, Guderian said, “That bloodline is only a legend. The Ice Sea Copper Pillar Inscription says the Black King Nidhogg destroyed the White King with supreme power: killed it, ate its flesh, turned its bones to ice, melted the ice and poured it into a volcano, annihilating body and soul. If it no longer exists, its Yanling has lost its power.”

“The White King’s rebellion was the greatest in dragon history. A third of the dragons rebelled. After suppressing them, the Black King recorded their fate on a heaven-high copper pillar—the inscription we found in Greenland,” Manstein said. “That makes it history written by Nidhogg’s faction. If dragons have political considerations, the Black King would certainly stress to his subjects that the rebel leader had been utterly destroyed. But could the soul of a first-generation dragon, the purest of dragon blood, really be erased so easily? Perhaps it still sleeps somewhere, like the other dragon princes.”
“We’ve never found a single descendant of the White King. Its branch was close to humans. If Lu Mingfei belongs to it, that needn’t be bad,” Guderian said.

Manstein lit his pipe, drew deeply several times, and smiled bitterly. “Don’t fool yourself. Neither of us believes it would help humanity. The first of the Three Principles of Dragons: dragons and humans are fundamentally different beings. The gulf between us is far greater than the hatred between the Black and White Kings. The inscription says it ‘stained its silver throne with the blood of the lowborn,’ suggesting its savagery. Perhaps it merely used humans to compensate for its deficiencies. The Black King created it, and it was weaker. But it remained alien. It could never truly sympathize with humanity.”
Guderian paled and fell silent. The antique wall clock ticked.
“We aren’t entirely human ourselves,” he said at last. “Does Black King blood or White King blood matter so much? Must we force bloodline theory on a child?”

Manstein puffed hard. “Have you considered the consequences of protecting him? If the White King was the ‘Savage King’ its creator described, who knows how its descendants would treat humans? Once his blood awakens, Lu Mingfei could become our enemy. Chu’s golden eyes can’t suppress him. His potential may be unmatched. Who would dare let him live here?”
“What are you saying?” Guderian raised his head sharply and demanded.
“Write a report. Submit it to the principal,” Manstein said quietly.
A chill entered Guderian’s heart. “What would such a report mean?”

“Isolate and study him. Until his identity is established, he can’t remain a student or leave the college. Don’t hesitate. Call now. Don’t implicate yourself.” Manstein took out his phone and offered it.
After a long silence, Guderian gripped his hand and slowly, firmly closed the phone.
“Lu Mingfei…” He paused, finally saying the words he had already settled on. “…is a very good boy.”

Manstein stared, baffled. Academically, he was Guderian’s inferior. He had copied his homework from their undergraduate days right through their doctorates. A casual remark from his friend might conceal profound meaning. He mustn’t expose his ignorance now. He needed to consider before replying.
He lowered his head in thought. The clock ticked. Seconds and minutes passed.
“You mean… the goodness of his human side will resist the White King’s summons?” he ventured. “All right. I give up. Tell me.”
Guderian scratched his head. “I… didn’t mean anything special. I just remember Nono saying he cried his eyes out in the ladies’ room after getting a letter from his parents.”
“Does that have anything to do with the White King’s bloodline?”

“No. I think he’s a lonely child, and kind. A good boy. We can’t deprive him of his chance. Who wants to be a specimen?” Guderian looked into his friend’s eyes. “We remember our childhoods, don’t we? We were specimens, too. Reaching through iron bars, trying so hard to hold each other’s hand… Weren’t you sad then, too?”
Manstein froze. Head lowered, he stared silently at his phone. Shouts traveled back across the decades into his ears:
“Separate those two crazy children! What are they doing?”
“Damn it! Let go! I’m warning you, don’t make trouble!”
“Time for electrotherapy! Pull them apart! Take him to the treatment room!”

He still remembered the pain, like broken blades cutting inside his body. After each great jolt, a faint scorched smell made him want to cry. He had stared at the solitary square window of his isolation cell, longing to fly like a bird, longing for something to descend from heaven and change his life.
Fingel tossed the stripped goose bone onto his plate, belched, and leaned forward to look Lu Mingfei in the eye. “Want to hear… a secret technique?”
“A secret technique?” Lu Mingfei paused.
Fingel lowered his voice. “Every exam is a means to an end. Means are invented by people. Anything people invent has a flaw!”
“Dear senior!” Lu Mingfei perked up, choosing his warmest form of address. “Do you have a plan?”
“Any objection to cheating?” Fingel’s eyes gleamed.
“Not… the slightest!”
“Promising material!” Fingel admired his resolve. “Remember, to survive here, we must have standards!”
“Standards?” Lu Mingfei couldn’t believe so moral a word had emerged from Fingel’s mouth.
“They must stand about three meters below ground level!” Fingel placed his hand on the floor. “Here. Dig down three meters. That’s our standard!”
“Makes perfect sense!” His senior had moved him deeply.

“In this place crawling with geniuses and lunatics, have standards, but never above minus three meters. Otherwise you’re doomed.” Fingel looked conspiratorial. “A craftsman sharpens his tools first. To cheat, we must understand what we’re cheating on! Junior, how many Draconic sentences have been deciphered?”
“Don’t you count words?”

“Wrong! Sentences! Only seventy-six!” Fingel assumed a lecturer’s manner. “Language has vocabulary and grammar. Together, they produce infinitely many sentences. But Draconic is a dead script. Only the characters survive, not the grammar. The last person who knew that grammar was Nicolas Flamel…”
“Nic… Nic… Nico-what?” Lu Mingfei hadn’t caught it.

“That pig brain! Forget it. Call him… Old Nick! We’ll call him Old Nick!” Fingel waved. “He lived in Paris, a scribe by trade and an alchemist. The only person in recorded history to create the Philosopher’s Stone!”
“The Philosopher’s Stone? Sounds cool.”

“Extremely! A little complicated to explain. Basically, a fifth element beyond earth, water, air, and fire: pure spirit. You’ll learn about it in Introduction to Alchemical Principles. Alchemy and Yanling are the twin pillars of dragon technology. Before science, dragons used them to work miracles. Old Nick’s interesting. A scribe, then suddenly a master of this dragon art. While copying a unique old book, he found an alchemical manuscript recording Draconic grammar. He learned it, but never passed it on. Instead, he compiled seventy-six obscure sentences and left only those to posterity. They’re all we can decipher today. Understand? At most, seventy-six possible questions.”
“You mean there’s a question bank?” Understanding dawned.

“Exactly! First, how the questions work. You enter the room and get blank paper and a pencil. No prompts. They play recordings of Draconic chanting. For dragon descendants, it resonates with the mind, producing spirit vision. Draconic is pictographic. You’ll ‘see’ incredible things.”
“See what?”
“Different for everyone. Usually tangled lines, writhing snakes, wildly growing plants, things like that. Just record what you see.”
“An art exam?” Lu Mingfei stared. “I’m not much of an artist.”

“If you can doodle a turtle, that’s enough. They’re testing spirit vision, not drawing skill. The purer the blood, the more you see and the more lifelike it is.” Fingel took blank paper and rapidly sketched with a pencil. Unexpectedly, he was good. Lu Mingfei watched a drawing emerge, extremely abstract, countless overlapping waveforms resembling an ocean from a distance.

“There are lots of curves here. Extract certain sections…” Fingel darkened several lines. “…and you get Draconic characters. Norma grades it. She analyzes your drawing in detail and locates them, very precisely. Random scribbles won’t work. This is something I drew back then. One of the questions.”
“So… seventy-six drawings? And variations on each? I can’t memorize that question bank!” Lu Mingfei’s newly kindled hope threatened to go out.
“Don’t worry. Now I reveal the ultimate secret!” Fingel bared his teeth in a grin. “The greatest flaw in Cassell’s 3E system: they reuse old papers!”
“Reuse?”
“Only eight papers in all. An eight-year cycle. They never change!”
“Have the professors lost their minds?” Lu Mingfei couldn’t believe it.

In China, teachers fought students and students fought teachers, both seasoned combatants. The entrance exam covered only a few textbooks, but what high school teacher couldn’t produce a hundred mock exams? Chinese teachers practiced something like Huang Yaoshi’s Jade Flute Swordplay, variation after variation, hundreds of moves. Cassell’s professors apparently favored the Eighteen Dragon-Subduing Palms: tremendous strength and force, but once the sequence ended, they had to start again.

Fingel shrugged. “Only a few dozen to a hundred take 3E each year. Geniuses. They graduate in four years and join the Executive Department, hunting dragon ruins worldwide. Who would memorize the papers and leak them to freshmen? An eight-year cycle is safe. But there’s always an exception.” He raised his brows, looking thoroughly sleazy. “Remember? I’ve been here eight years!”
“Aaaaaah!” Enlightenment struck. Lu Mingfei was beside himself. “This year’s paper is exactly the one you took when you arrived!”

“Three thousand dollars, no bargaining. Deferred payment accepted. Subtract the four hundred ninety-seven you spent treating me, plus two dollars’ Coke in Chicago. You owe twenty-five hundred and one. I’ll waive the odd dollar. Twenty-five hundred for my paper. Your decision. Ten-second countdown!” Fingel spoke like bullets leaving a barrel, his tone hard as a sword stroke. “Ten! Nine! Eight!…”
“Wait, wait… Hey! What’s going on?” Lu Mingfei panicked.
“Seven! Six!”
“At least let me inspect the goods, senior! You can’t force a sale!”
“Five! Four!”
“What if they’re not as advertised? Any repair, replacement, or refund guarantee? Do you issue receipts?”
“Three! Two!”
“Hey, bastard! Are you listening? Damn it… Deal!” Feeling almost faint, Lu Mingfei collapsed into a seat, panting.

“At this point, only I can help. You have no choice. Why resist?” Fingel drained his sparkling wine and exhaled a leisurely breath of carbon dioxide. “I knew these eight hard years wouldn’t be wasted. Today, for the first time, I turned knowledge into money!”
“Pah! Shameless! Crooked merchant!” Lu Mingfei was furious. “And I thought you were one of those idiot seniors with thick glasses, lots of knowledge, no girlfriend, and a one-track mind!”

“Nonsense! I was an A-rank as imposing here as Caesar! Plenty of girls admired me. Flirtatious emails in my college inbox!” Fingel thumped his broad chest, the German wearing the triumphant smile of a Jewish merchant closing a deal.
“Single old guys always brag about being irresistible in their youth!” Grieving for his twenty-five hundred dollars, which had just sprouted wings and flown away, Lu Mingfei struck back savagely.

Fingel looked downcast. “Unfortunately, I was determined to earn enough credits to graduate in three years and become the Executive Department’s youngest agent. I ignored their interest… By the time I wanted to respond, they’d all become little Executive Department birds and flown around the world.”
“A loser who keeps repeating years shouldn’t talk like that. Even if they hadn’t flown away, they’d only say, ‘I was so blind as a kid, liking Fingel.’”

“Junior.” Fingel patted his head. “Your first college lesson: girls fall for men through foolishness, and they’re more prone to foolishness when young. So cute little girls are better than glamorous older women!”

“Enough, enough. Stop the commentary. Twenty-five hundred? I don’t have it. Can I pay when the scholarship arrives?” Lu Mingfei asked. “And what four-hundred-ninety-seven-dollar treat? I don’t remember buying you anything that expensive.”
“Later payment’s fine. As for the meal…” Fingel tapped the goose bone against the plate. “Half’s in your stomach. Half’s in mine.”
“Wasn’t that the college’s late-night food service?” Lu Mingfei was lost.
“They charge! Think you eat off silver for free? A free meal gets you a plastic fork at best!”
“But we never paid, Senior Wisecrack!”
“We swiped your student ID.”
“My student ID?” Lu Mingfei was puzzled.

“It’s also a credit card guaranteed by Citibank. As S-rank aristocracy, you have a hundred-thousand-dollar limit. Doesn’t treating your useless senior, with his eighty-dollar remaining limit, to a four-hundred-ninety-seven-dollar meal seem wonderfully generous?”
“So… I’ve already started going into debt?” His heart bled.
“Debt’s nothing to fear.” Fingel reassured him. “I’m over thirty thousand in the red, and living quite nicely.”
Lu Mingfei covered his face. His senior’s serene shamelessness left him in despair.
Midnight. Beneath the library, a red access-control light blinked at a steady frequency, signaling that the security system was operating normally.

It was quiet, broken only occasionally by spinning hard drives. The enormous central computer occupied the first through sixth basement levels. Aboveground, it would have been the size of a small building. Security was at the highest level: retinal, voiceprint, and fingerprint recognition all active. Blast-resistant alloy plates formed the outer walls. Infrared lasers scanned every area, even gaps admitting only a mouse.

Footsteps approached, sounding like iron-shod military boots. The red light blinked faster, increasingly so as they drew nearer. Unable to identify the visitor from the footsteps, the system raised its threat rating toward the alarm threshold.
The footsteps stopped at the entrance. Ignoring the biometric systems, the visitor swiped an unmarked black card through the slot.

The threat rating plummeted. Infrared scanners and hundreds of cameras powered down. Warning lights turned green. With faint clicks, all nine metal doors leading to the central computer unlocked together.

On the library’s top floor, Manstein and Guderian faced each other silently. Manstein glanced at his watch and froze. It was a monitoring terminal. It showed the security system entering sleep mode, though that system ran year-round and never slept.
“Executive Department. Norma’s security system has gone dormant. Send people to the library.” Still speaking, Manstein ran for the elevator.
Guderian set down the sealed Ice Sea Fragment vessel and squeezed in just as the doors closed.
At the ground floor, Manstein stepped out and looked around. Deep in the night, the floor was silent.

Cassell’s library was an elegant building in antique style, with a ground-floor hall nearly ten meters high, magnificent as the Sistine Chapel. Exquisite marble columns supported graceful vaults, beneath stained-glass windows through which the starry sky could be seen. Polished granite tiles reflected visitors like mirrors. The carved cherrywood doors at the corridor’s end were locked.
A knock sounded. Manstein opened the door to a tall, gaunt figure standing in shadow, dressed entirely in black and pulling a small cart.
“Professor von Schneider. You came yourself,” Manstein said.
“Mans is in China. I have to attend to things personally.” Schneider raised a hand in greeting. “I noticed Norma’s security system sleeping, too.”

He entered the light. A black mask covered his face; an air hose led to a steel cylinder on the cart. Dark-red scars crowded his neck. His breathing was low and clogged, like damaged bellows. Iron-gray eyes swept coldly across them.
Both professors looked away. Nobody at Cassell liked meeting the Executive Department chief’s eyes. It felt like staring at a blade point from a few centimeters away.
“No intruder detected on surveillance.” Schneider glanced around, then turned to Manstein. “It’s late. You two are the only ones here. Anything unusual?”

“Nothing. The 3E exam’s tomorrow. Perhaps students are trying to hack Norma for the paper.” Manstein forced a smile, attempting to lighten the atmosphere. The Executive Department always carried itself rather imperiously. As Disciplinary Committee chairman, he dealt with students and preferred avoiding the department unless necessary. Still, he had to show Schneider some respect.
“Students stealing exam papers aren’t our concern. Pureblood dragons are.” Schneider ignored the smile entirely. “Norma’s security cannot be breached. It’s designed as an endless loop.”
“If dragons invaded, surely the computer room wouldn’t be their target?” Guderian asked.
“Unknown. Dragons cannot be understood. Vigilance is never wrong.” Schneider raised his voice. “Norma. Why is security dormant?”

The overhead crystal chandelier suddenly lit, clean brilliance dispelling the cold darkness. Rows of carved cherrywood shelves filled the magnificent hall, holding hundreds of thousands of reference books. Brass plaques marked their sections. Identical green-shaded lamps on long cherrywood tables lit in succession. Not a shadow remained. The hall was empty.

“Professor von Schneider, Professor Manstein, Professor Guderian. Routine cleaning. I’m clearing junk data. I paused security and opened the data shield to send it out.” A composed female voice echoed overhead. “Simply put, I opened the door to take out the trash.”
“So much redundant data that you need a midnight cleanup? Opening the door creates a vulnerability. You should do it with other personnel present,” Schneider said.
“Until dragons learn to use computers, I believe I’m safe,” Norma replied.
“They learn quickly. Be careful.” He was noticeably kinder to her than to his colleagues. “How much longer?”
“Just finished. Security is back online. The next disposal is in seventeen years. Until then, I’m completely secure.”
“Sounds like seventeen years without nighttime library patrols.” He laughed hoarsely. “We won’t disturb you further. Good night, madam.”
“Good night, gentlemen.” Chandelier and desk lamps dimmed, leaving only a few warm-yellow iron wall sconces.

Schneider turned to go, then looked back at the two professors. “Access logs show you entered the rare-books section. Those books are highly classified. What academic problem brought you here to study them at this hour?”

Beneath his clouded but icy gaze, goose bumps rose all over Guderian. He looked desperately to Manstein, who still held the phone with which, minutes earlier, he had meant to report the White King descendant to the principal.
“Something you can’t discuss?” Schneider pressed coldly.

Cold sweat covered Guderian’s forehead. He feared Manstein would mention Lu Mingfei. He wasn’t good at lying himself. As his friend said, whenever he lied, he couldn’t stop scratching his head. Schneider was hard to fool. Before leading the department, he had been an excellent scholar.
“The White King,” Manstein said softly.
Guderian’s head buzzed. He couldn’t protect Lu Mingfei. It was over.
“The White King?” Schneider’s eyes widened. The name clearly struck hard.
“A new hypothesis.” Manstein lowered his voice and leaned toward his ear. “The White King may be female!”
“Female?” Schneider’s eyes widened further. After a long consideration, he asked, “How did you reach that conclusion?”
Guderian looked blankly from one to the other.

“I’ve been considering the cause of the dragons’ civil war. Human rulers fight over land, gold, or women. What did dragons fight over? Land and gold mean little to them. Could a female dragon have triggered it?” Manstein spoke fluently and gravely.
“Hmm!” Schneider nodded repeatedly. “A fresh approach.”

“Conflict between the sexes: such an important theme in human history! We’ve never considered whether the White and Black Kings’ conflict was gender rather than power. Many examples exist of a husband and wife both wielding power but holding differing positions, leading to serious disputes. For example…” Manstein suddenly faltered. “For example…”
“Hillary and Clinton!” Schneider supplied.

“Exactly! Hillary and Clinton!” Manstein clapped his shoulder forcefully. “Imagine this research premise: the Black King created the White King to be his wife. Daughters marrying fathers are commonplace in Greek mythology. Their conflict as male and female ultimately caused the split.”
“A rather human interpretation, but should we include the marital relationship in our research?” Schneider mused.
“An excellent point!” Manstein said. “Perhaps we could share the project, all three of us. Though when we publish, would you expect first authorship?”
“No, no, nothing of the sort.” Schneider waved hastily. “I’m merely interested. An excellent angle!”
“Then shall we assemble detailed materials and discuss it together?” Manstein asked solemnly.
“Wonderful. Interesting, very interesting. A project worth losing sleep over.” Schneider shook his hand and left, thinking as he walked, until he vanished into the distant dark.
“The White King might be female?” Guderian looked at Manstein.
“Made it up.” Manstein cut him off impatiently. “Had to give Schneider something novel and interesting to ponder. Otherwise we’d have to explain accessing classified documents at midnight.”
“But your argument made sense…”

“Enough!” Manstein covered his friend’s mouth. “I said I made it up! We won’t know the White King’s sex anytime soon. But I’ll give your student a chance. Tomorrow is 3E. Black King and White King descendants have very different Yanling. If Lu Mingfei is of the Black King’s blood, he’ll do well. Then forget my theory completely.”
“And if… he fails?” Guderian asked.
Manstein sighed. “Then we must report it. Guderian… I know what you’re like. But you must know we have no right to be selfish.”
“All right.” Guderian sighed. “Still, thank you.”
“Nothing. You’re right. If I were him, I wouldn’t want to be treated as an alien either,” Manstein said. “We suffered enough of that. Let’s hope it doesn’t happen to the children.”

Guderian left last. Holding the cherrywood door handle, he suddenly remembered something. He had locked it upon entering. But when Manstein let Schneider in, he didn’t seem to have turned the brass handle three times the other way… He couldn’t remember clearly, and was too tired. Shaking his head, he pulled the door closed behind him.
Forty meters beneath the library, a figure huddled in a swivel chair, hands tucked away, head bowed. Only monitors lit the room, leaving his face in shadow.
“Everyone else has gone. During the security pause, the cameras were off. There’s no record of your entry,” Norma said. “I’ll pause it again when you leave. What brings you here?”
“Can’t I visit an old friend?” The man smiled, his newly shaved chin blue-dark. “Activate the EVA personality.”
“Do appearances matter that much? I’m still me. Norma or EVA, at the deepest level, I’m still me,” she said.

The enormous screen darkened, leaving countless little red and green lights blinking. Vast quantities of personality data flooded the supercomputer like seawater rushing upstream. Drive lights, data-traffic indicators, and processor-frequency lights flashed ten times faster, then faster still, until an almost frenzied frequency set the entire basement’s rhythm.
Suddenly, every light went out. Absolute darkness filled the basement.

A beam descended from directly overhead, striking the floor before the chair. Luminous fragments drifted within it like snow. A girl stood at its center, translucent, shimmering faintly. Long black hair fell to her feet, though its ends floated in the air. She wore a long silk dress like a nightgown, barefoot and smiling.
“EVA.” Slowly, the man reached into the light.
“All you can touch is air. Why reach out?” she asked softly.
“I just like holding your hand. It’s a habit.” Luminous fragments landed on his palm and vanished instantly.

EVA laid her translucent hand over his, offering no sensation. Mere illusions of light and shadow, departed memories preserved by 3D imaging. He gently closed his hand on emptiness, as though truly holding a girl’s hand.
“Sometimes you used to hold my hand for more than ten hours a day. When you let go, our hands were covered in sweat,” she said.
“If I didn’t hold it, how would I know you were there?”
“You’ve always been so insecure. What use is strength to you?”
“I’m only lonely.”
After a long silence, EVA asked, “Did you come to tell me something?”
“To ask a favor. I want this year’s S-rank freshman, Lu Mingfei, to pass 3E, whatever his actual potential.”
“If he really has no dragon blood, letting him pass and enter could expose our secrets.”
“Call it a favor for a friend. It isn’t difficult for you.”
“For Norma, you mean.” EVA sighed softly.
“Are you Norma?” He looked at the small, translucent hand in his. “I can’t feel your hand. Often I think you aren’t really here anymore.”
“I’m not here anymore,” she whispered. “What you see is only your own memory.”
After a long silence, he said, “You’re all-powerful here. I’d like a beer.”
“Only hard drives, processors, and routers here. No beer. After all these years, you’ve changed so much. Still can’t change that bad drinking habit?”

“I thought I’d never drink again… If I hadn’t been drunk that night, perhaps I wouldn’t have lost you.” His voice was hoarse. “But all these years, I still need alcohol. When I don’t drink, I think of you. I hate memories. They always make it hard to tell who I am.”
“You’re yourself. You’ve never changed.”

“Hee-ha, hee-ha, hee-ha!” came from behind him. He turned warily, veins bulging and twisting like snakes along his forearms as unparalleled strength gathered. What he saw was strange: a little humanoid made of metal spheres and short rods, only knee-high. Components that should have lain scattered seemed held together by powerful magnetism. It even had a comical clown’s face. Two metal-bead eyes rolled about; a rod mouth spread in an ingratiating smile. On the tray in its “hands” sat a chilled bottle of Samuel Adams dark beer.
As he took the bottle, the little creature deftly produced an opener and popped the cap.
“Have a pleasant evening, sir.” Its voice issued from the surrounding speakers, in a bartender’s tone.
“I made it when I was bored. It’s the only one who plays with me here,” EVA said. “Its name is Adams.”
“You named it after a beer… Or do you think it’s your Adam? To go with your EVA—Eve in German.” He sipped and waved at Adams. “You can go now, little fellow.”
Its smile grew cuter. It remained behind him, holding the tray.
“It likes tips,” EVA said.
“You know how poor I am.” Muttering, he took several quarters from his pocket and dropped them on the tray.
Adams bowed happily, chattered its cheerful “Hee-ha, hee-ha, hee-ha!” and darted into the dark.
“I meant to name it after you, but thought you might object,” EVA said.
“Am I that ugly?” He shrugged. “Could I also hear what the Executive Department’s people are planning lately?”
“Your real purpose?” She sighed. “Covering for a freshman is one thing. Leaking operational plans is another.”
“You’ll tell me. You’ve always granted my requests,” he whispered.

After a silence, she said, “Four additional teams have gone to Tibet, Xinjiang, Greenland, and Mexico. Roughly thirteen hundred people worldwide are searching for dragon tombs. Professor Mans’s team is closest to success. Its target is Norton, King of Bronze and Fire, a noble first-generation dragon and one of the Four Monarchs. They’ll conduct Operation Kuimen on the Yangtze. I don’t know the details. The principal devised it personally.”
“Who besides Mans is involved? Norton’s exceptional even among first-generation dragons. Hard to kill.”
“Ye Sheng and Aki Sakatoku, the strongest young partnership in the department. The principal arranged it. There shouldn’t be a mistake.”
“He’s made mistakes before. For instance… ten years ago,” the man said faintly.
“Ten years. Don’t keep holding on. We paid dearly, but we won.”
“But only I came back alive.” He swirled the bottle.
“We’re all still watching over you, just like before!” EVA placed her other hand on his shoulder.

Several beams appeared around him, each containing a translucent figure: a girl in leather with neat, short red hair; a cold boy in sunglasses; a black-clad man with a monk’s solemn face; a charming girl with her head tilted and long hair swirling. Six people in all, including EVA. They laid hands on his shoulders and smiled together, like smiles in an old photograph, still brilliant after so many years.
Head lowered, he drank in silence, neither looking at them nor speaking.

“EVA, don’t play games like this.” He shook his head. “They aren’t here. They’re asleep under the icy sea, thousands of kilometers away, locked in those metal diving suits… Unable to die, yet unable ever to come back.”
The other beams vanished. Only EVA remained, stroking his cheek with an insubstantial hand.
“Any news of the Crown Prince?” he asked.
“If he’s alive, he should be Emperor by now. But I have no news.”
“Of course he’s alive. I can still smell his rotten stench. Besides, if he were dead, how could I kill him myself?” His voice was as cold as the words were vicious.
“If killing him is the only way you can find peace,” EVA whispered, “then… kill him. I’ll wait for your news.”

He nodded and withdrew his hand from the emptiness. He had only held air all along. Tipping back the beer, he headed out. Invisible to the naked eye, the web of infrared scanners shut down. Cameras automatically switched off. Flashing red warning lights turned green. High-voltage electricity beneath the corridor floor was cut. Security entered another brief sleep.
“Oh, right. That matter with Lu Mingfei. No problem?” Remembering, he turned back.
“No problem. Just covering for a freshman. It’s hardly the only bad thing I’ve helped you do.” EVA smiled. “May I ask why?”
“He seems a decent kid.” He smiled, too. “I have other reasons. I’ll tell you when I’ve confirmed my ideas.”

He turned away, took two steps, stopped, and approached Adams in the corner. Crouching, he said, “Hey, brother. Could you return two coins so I can buy a Coke… I gave you everything… Look, money’s only a toy to you. No supermarket or Coke machine down here…”
Adams’s expression changed. Clutching its coins, it looked the perfect miser.
“Adams, give your big brother two coins,” EVA said.
Its face changed again, deeply aggrieved. Carefully, it selected two old coins and handed them over.
“What a little miser!” He clapped its head hard. The alchemically constructed puppet robot couldn’t withstand the force and collapsed into a heap of metal rods and spheres rolling everywhere.
Tossing the two coins and drinking his beer, the man receded. EVA silently watched his burly, lonely back. It wasn’t as straight as it had been ten years ago.
The metal doors opened and closed. The man was truly gone. In the beam of light, the girl began to cry without a sound.

Rods and spheres rolled together. Adams reassembled itself and ran over, chattering “Hee-ha, hee-ha, hee-ha!” It froze at her illusory tears. After a moment, it suddenly waved both hands above its head and shook its body in an ungainly dance. “EVA, be happy! EVA, be happy! EVA, be happy!”
Coins clattered from its hands across the floor. Her tears fell onto the metal as well, splashing into faint blue glimmers.
“A freshman taking six of the top ten headlines in one day. Unimaginable.”
“He killed Caesar and Chu. Imagine if his gun had held live rounds instead of Frigga rounds…”
“Breaking: S-Rank Lu Mingfei Has No Resonance with the Dragon Emperor’s Secret Incantation. College Investigates!”
“Who Claims the Freedom Day Crown? Who Blew Away Caesar, Then Chu Zihang?”

Manstein shook his head and closed the college forum. It would probably be a sleepless night. Online numbers had reached a new high. Students across the college, even teachers using aliases, were hotly debating the freshman Lu Mingfei. Would a new S-rank bring hope, danger, or merely ridicule?
Manstein was uncertain, too. The White King theory might be unreliable. It was only conjecture, after all. No descendant had ever been documented.
All he had was an instinctive wariness of the Lu Mingfei who shot Caesar and Chu.
He turned off the light, sat alone in darkness for a while, then opened his phone and called. “Father.”
The forum refreshed rapidly, messages scrolling upward without pause.
“Maybe 3E will put him in his place tomorrow. He doesn’t look capable. Perhaps the principal misjudged his rank,” someone posted.
“Maybe he has no dragon blood at all, so Chu’s golden eyes don’t scare him.”
“His greatest strength is competitive gaming! What a joke of a talent!”

“Hey! Let’s open a book. Who’s betting he fails 3E tomorrow?” Fingel posted, an administrator badge beside his name. His arrival stirred excitement. This useless senior who could never graduate was a campus celebrity. He ran the news channel and always found something sensational.
“Not many will bet he passes. I’ll start. A hundred says he does!” He opened a topic in the polling section.
“Fingel, are you staking your chance of paying off your credit card on your roommate?” someone mocked.

The No-side stakes soared, soon passing twenty thousand dollars. On Yes, only Fingel’s hundred remained. In one short evening, everyone had unearthed Lu Mingfei’s background: laughable grades, no girlfriend because nobody wanted him, a terrible sense of direction, gaming his only talent, dozens of pirated discs confiscated at customs. From any angle, a loser, nothing like an S-rank of legendary blood purity and boundless potential.
“Does nobody have a gambling spirit?” Fingel complained. “This is no fun. All you can win is my hundred. Right now, a bet on his passing pays a hundred thirty to one!”
“Five hundred says he passes,” posted an ID called Murasame.

The forum fell silent. Chu Zihang’s ID rarely appeared there. Lionheart’s quiet president, the super-A-rank, disliked endless chatter. Yet he had made an exception to gamble five hundred on Lu Mingfei passing.
“I bet five thousand,” posted Dictator.
“Caesar!” someone exclaimed.
“On his failing.” Caesar logged off, leaving the forum temporarily frozen.

Dimly, another contest had begun. If natural enemies truly existed, Caesar and Chu were surely examples. Students couldn’t remember them agreeing on anything. Today, at last, they had: after a freshman’s two shots miraculously ended Freedom Day, both presidents accepted the result.

Would they admit defeat to a loser? Surrender a year’s use of Norton Hall and the right to pursue any girl without rejection? Students thought them almost too generous. Neither needed to fear romantic failure, of course. Quiet, reserved Chu remained single and apparently uninterested in women. Caesar already had the famous Nono.

Holding a wireless keyboard, Caesar reclined on the sofa in Amber Hall’s lounge and watched the stakes climb on a huge projection screen. After leaving Dictator, he had logged in as Sonic, an inconspicuous ID tucked silently into a corner of the online list.
With an iced coffee, Nono leaned against the wall behind him. “You’re paying a lot of attention to Lu Mingfei.”
“Yes. I don’t know whether he’ll pass tomorrow,” Caesar admitted freely. “I bet against him only because I never take Chu Zihang’s side in a wager.”
“I know. Five thousand means nothing to you.” She set down the coffee and picked up her backpack. “I’m off. I chose Manstein’s course this semester. Need to hit the books. Call if anything comes up.”

“Won’t that tiny room with Susie feel cramped for studying? Besides, she shot you today… She’d do anything for Chu.” Caesar reached out as if to stop her. “Stay here. Amber Hall’s even more comfortable than Norton.”
At the door, Nono turned and rolled her eyes.
He hastily raised both hands, protesting innocence. “I mean… a guest room! I have plenty!”
“What I like least about you is renting villas on campus. Doesn’t it feel empty?” She curled her lip. “I don’t like your Bugatti either.”
“Fortunately, I lost it today.” He shrugged.
“Oh. Good boy.” She pulled the door closed. Caesar pushed his fingers into his brilliant blond hair and scratched his head, helpless.

“Three minutes until betting closes! Place your bets now. All stakes must reach my account before tomorrow’s 3E exam. I’ll hold them. Otherwise, the bet is void.” Curled on a common-room sofa in Dormitory Area One, Fingel cradled his laptop, fingers flying. A dozen or so students surrounded him, solemnly watching.

“The power of news! First I leak his lack of Draconic resonance. Then I open a book on his passing 3E.” Fingel applauded himself gleefully. “Then the mastermind bets he passes. At least fivefold profit. I move myself. Stakes ready?”
“Ready,” a mathematician-like boy answered.
“Wait until just before the close. Otherwise they’ll catch on.”
“Understood. Thirty-four seconds! Synchronized with system time!” An elite member of the campus loan-sharking ring opened a countdown program, replying with a scientist’s precision.
“Three or four seconds early. The odds are already fixed. Most money will come in at the end. There may be lag,” someone warned.
Stakes changed rapidly on both sides, new bets arriving every second. Closing time approached. Their hearts raced like traders’ on a stock exchange.
“Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four…” The timekeeper licked his slightly dry lips.
“Place it! Close!” Fingel swept his arm commandingly.
“Zero!” the timekeeper shouted. “Bet placed! We win!”
“Wait! The amount on Lu Mingfei is… thirty-nine thousand four hundred. Someone put in twenty thousand at the last second…” A voice trembled.
“Twenty thousand!” Fingel was aghast. “Use my administrator ID. Find out who!”
A minute later, he stared at the laptop. The bettor’s ID was perfectly clear, his real name, open and unashamed: Gerd Rudolf Manstein. Followed by his title: Professor.
“The Disciplinary Committee chairman gambles, too… Isn’t he supposed to stop cheating?” Cold sweat poured from Fingel.

Meanwhile, under a lamp, Lu Mingfei copied the answer sheet Fingel had left, stroke by stroke. His senior had gone out wearing a strange smile, saying he didn’t want to interrupt his efforts. Lu Mingfei was alone. Less than four hours until dawn. In that time, he had to copy eight drawings and commit them to memory. The lines were dense forests of tangled vines, never meant to be remembered.
But remember them he must, even as fatigue rose slowly like a tide.

What if the goods weren’t as advertised? What if this twenty-five-hundred-dollar answer sheet was nonsense? Who tested a language by drawing pictures? Why trust Fingel, alternately clueless and cunning? The man had exploited him from beginning to end. His thoughts tangled. And what if he passed? In a college of geniuses boasting reptilian ancestry, would he crawl out alive? Then what? Travel the world killing dragons?
Far away in China, it should be morning. Was Chen Wenwen in her white dress, holding her new boyfriend’s hand on their way to some ordinary university?
That night Nono drove him down the elevated road, he had thought he had found a way out. Yet he was still a tiny firefly, following everyone else in aimless flight.
Hugging his knees on the bed, he thought for a long time, then whispered to himself, “Nono, I really want to see you.”
He just wanted to see her, whatever had happened.
